sources.citation: Díaz Romero, Camilo Enrique. 2023. Sobre las lenguas indígenas habladas en las zonas Andina y los Llanos Orientales de Colombia: propuesta de clasificaciones desde la tipología areal. Literatura y Lingüística 48 (ICC Biblioteca Digital eprint 1881).
sources.note: Areal-typological feature comparison that uses Tobar (2000b) as its Tinigua source; no accent/stress feature is coded for any language; silent on Tinigua stress.

sources.citation: English Wikipedia, 'Tinigua language' (phonology section summarising Bolaños 2023: pp.1037ff.)
sources.note: Gives Bolaños's consonant/vowel charts, phonotactics (CV, CVC; CVV from phonetic word-final lengthening) and example forms with acute accents (ɲísa, kʰakʰá, hatsamí-j), but says nothing about stress placement.

sources.citation: Adelaar, Willem F. H. with Pieter C. Muysken. 2004. The Languages of the Andes (Cambridge Language Surveys). Cambridge: CUP. [short Tinigua section summarising Tobar Ortiz]
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Dumbarton Oaks Library, call number PM5100.A34 2004X; Tozzer Library, call number S.A. Ad 32 l)
sources.harvard_location: Dumbarton Oaks Library, call number PM5100 .A34 2004X; Tozzer Library, call number S.A. Ad 32 l
sources.note: Accessible-in-libraries English summary of Tobar Ortiz's phonology; would give a citable second-hand stress remark if Tobar made one.

sources.citation: SAPhon (South American Phonological Inventory Database), inventory page 'Tinigua' (source: Tobar 2000).
sources.note: Segment inventory after Tobar 2000 (aspirated/plain/voiced stops, 6 vowels each with glottalized and long counterparts); field 'Suprasegmental: None' (SAPhon codes tone/nasal harmony there, not stress placement). No stress statement.

sources.citation: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Idioma tinigua' (inventory after Tobar Ortiz 1994/1995)
sources.note: Six oral vowels each with glottalized and lengthened counterparts, 22 consonants; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Castellví, Marcelino de. 1940. La lengua tinigua. Journal de la Société des Américanistes 32(1): 93-101. doi:10.3406/jsa.1940.2324 (Persée; per-page scanned text harvested, PDF download blocked by altcha captcha)
sources.note: Nothing. p.95 has only a note on the phonetic notation (Institut d'Ethnologie system, vowel o/u instability); pp.96-101 are a Spanish-Tinigua wordlist from Capuchin missionaries with acute accents written on forms (e.g. ñikwáiši 'agua', číña 'jaguar', ťóka 'maíz') but no rule or remark on accent placement.

sources.citation: Bolaños, Katherine. 2023. Tinigua. In P. Epps & L. Michael (eds.), Amazonian Languages: Language Isolates II: Kanoé to Yurakaré (HSK 44.2), 1029-1075. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.

sources.citation: Bolaños, Katherine (depositor). 2017-. Documentation of Tinigua / Documentación del idioma tinigua. London: Endangered Languages Archive (ELAR), collection dk0464 (ELDP postdoctoral project 'Linguistic Documentation of Tinigua', host University of Texas at Austin, funder Arcadia; earlier ELAR address elar.soas.ac.uk/Collection/MPI1079925). Audio-visual corpus of Tinigua narratives recorded with the last speaker Sixto Muñoz, with transcription/translation, a preliminary grammatical sketch and a c. 500-item lexicon.
sources.tag: likely states tone; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: online with restricted access (login, paywall or limited view); the linked copy could not be retrieved
sources.note: Nothing about tone, stress or pitch is stated in any record seen (CIC project page, ELDP project list, search-engine summary of the ELAR landing page); the collection is primary audio-visual material plus a preliminary grammatical sketch and lexicon, i.e. the only first-hand data on Tinigua prosody besides the known, unobtained Bolaños 2023 HSK chapter. The claim that Bolaños 2023 reports penultimate stress and no tone comes from a tertiary AI page and is not part of this record.
